title: Sunscreen SPF50

drivers.name: Promotion (30% off)
drivers.evidence: Past 30% off promotion: noise-adjusted uplift x1.02; this is deeper than usual (25% max), but evidence is thin (1 occurrence).

drivers.name: Store closure (Monday)
drivers.evidence: Store closed Monday; 1/7 of selling days lost. No prior closure data, but impact is structural.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 24.9. A 30% discount (price drop to $9.75 from $13.38) is deeper than past promotions (max 25% off), but the noise-adjusted uplift from past 30% off is only x1.02. The store closure on Monday (a full day) reduces the selling window by 1/7 (~14%), but no past closure data exists. The holiday effect (Thanksgiving week) is not directly relevant as this is after the holiday. The classical model suggests +2%, but past promotion effects are noisy and already shrunk. We apply a conservative uplift of +2% for the promotion, reduce by ~14% for the closure, netting 1.02 * 0.86 = 0.88. The noise-adjusted evidence is weak, so we shrink toward 1.0. Final median: 0.90. Spreads remain at 1.0 as no new uncertainty is introduced.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 24.9 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 64.6 | 10%-90%: 1.6 - 44.4

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-77% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
